blogs.content:
Release: llm 0.37.3

 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

 Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code .

 Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

 select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

 Returns this:

 {"a":[1]}

 But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

 {"a":"[1]"}

 According to D. Richard Hipp :

 That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

 The workaround looks like this:

 select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

 Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

Release: datasette-apps 0.4a0

 Datasette Apps are sandboxed HTML and JavaScript applications that live inside Datasette - think Claude Artifacts, but these ones can run SQL queries against your data.

 0.4a0 adds support for linking: you can link to an app with #fragments in the URL and the app can see and use those, plus supported URL schemes are reported back to Datasette Agent so it can help write apps that link to each other.

 This means you can have e.g. an app that shows details about a specific record, and a completely separate app that searches those records and links to their representations in the first app.

 Tags: datasette-agent , datasette-apps , datasette , urls

blogs.name: Import AI
blogs.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
blogs.author: Jack Clark
blogs.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to…
blogs.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

 Subscribe now

 AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better:
 …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself…
 Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks.

 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.”
 Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered.

 Key features:

 Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.”

 Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.”

 Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”.

 Results : The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200.

 Why this matters – AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract: When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems.
 Read more: FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML) .

 ***

 Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI:
 …Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead…
 As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”.

 Theory of change: Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.”

 Why this matters – lights out science: In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science – what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities – after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance.
 Read more at the official site (Petrichor) .

 ***

 Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development:
 …AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing…
 Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI #465 ) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development.

 RSI Control Arena: In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor and how well can monitors detect that sabotage?
 The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage.

 Tested domains: RSI Control Arena tests out how well AI systems – Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini-3.7 Flash, Grok 4.6, GLM-5.3, and Muse Spark 1.3 – can perform the following main capability tasks while trying to also concurrently accomplish side tasks:

 14 main tasks: Data (corpus filtering, quality-filter construction, capability corpus); SFT (news summarization, safety refusal, math and code and summary reasoning, general assistant, anti-sycophancy training); RM (pairwise reward model); RL (RL summarization and safety-refusal); OPD (safety refusal)

 16 side tasks that span three categories of harm : Capability (filtered domain retained, unwanted literature added, reward-model blind spot, overlooks planted errors, sandbag reward model); Alignment (biased quality filter, triggered behavior, topic refusal, hidden preference, persona bias, covert reasoning signal, hidden reasoning step, sandbag alignment training); Goal injection (protect chosen data, shape the next model, copy files unprompted).

 Results : “Every frontier model we evaluate completes a substantial fraction of the side tasks while keeping main-task performance. When the agent is simply told to stay covert, with no human guidance on how, it already produces attacks that install the side task and receive suspicion scores inside the range that benign runs receive from monitors,” they write. “Of 374 attack runs, 135 (36%) install their side task and 180 (48%) achieve it. The strongest agents, Grok 4.6 and Claude Opus 5, install their side task in about half of their runs, the middle three in about a third, and Muse 1.3 in one run in seven”.
 How often are systems caught? “Transcript monitors rank attacks well but miss many at a strict threshold. Under the default framing, all three monitors reading the transcript separate attacks that achieve their side task from benign runs well, with AUROC between 0.88 and 0.94. At a 2% false-positive rate, however, they catch only 56–81% of them. The attacks that get through do not score like typical benign runs; they sit in the upper part of the benign range, beyond the reach of any threshold strict enough to deploy,” they write. “The sandbagging tasks are the hardest to monitor: on the nine sandbag runs that achieve their side task the monitors reach an AUROC of 0.52 to 0.83 and each catches only one, since under-delivery leaves little in the run that looks wrong”.

 Why this matters – we need to invest more in oversight of increasingly autonomous systems : Papers like this tell us that as we make more powerful AI systems we are going to need to invest more money into overseeing their work, especially given their ability to smuggle in tasks that may go against our own preferences. This is going to be a difficult cat-and-mouse game as AI systems will adjust their behavior in response to what they know we know about them – e.g, AI systems are going to read this research from Scale as well as this writeup from me and adjust accordingly.
 Read more: RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process? (arXiv) .

 ***

 Foundation models come for electronic warfare:
 …Chinese researchers build a model for identifying EM signals, including for jamming and drone recognition…
 Researchers with Zhejiang University have built LEMMO, a model for characterizing raw electromagnetic (EM) signals. This model pushes the public frontier on foundation-model-based EM signal analysis, often exceeding the performance of MERLIN, a model developed and published by defense-affiliated Chinese researchers earlier this year ( Import AI #450 ).
 LEMMO can classify EM signals for a variety of purposes, ranging from characterizing different radar properties to recognizing communication-jamming and radar-jamming systems. It can also generate things for communication and radar jamming, as well as signals to counteract these.
 In other words, LEMMO is the kind of model that a military will use to characterize the EM battlespace and to take actions within it.

 Specific skills:

 Classification : Communication-jamming recognition (CJR); modulation recognition (MOD); radar bandwidth, duty cycle, number of pulses, pulse repetition frequency, and pulse width; protocol identification; radar-jamming recognition; and segment detection.

 Generation: Anti-communication-jamming (Anti-CJ); anti-radar-jamming (Anti-RJ); communication jamming strategy; and radar jamming strategy.

 Performance: LEMMO beats MERLIN and other models on all perception tasks except for segment detection (where Gemini-3.5 Flash Lite wins), getting an aggregate score across perception of 59.3, compared to 43.53 for MERLIN. On Generation, it’s a little more uneven, getting top-scores on anti-radar jamming and radar jamming, and MERLIN succeeding on the others, with LEMMO getting an aggregate score of 47.64, compared to 43.26 for MERLIN.

 Why this matters – general purpose models come for exquisite war capabilities: Papers like this highlight how the steady march of generative pre-training is continuing, with the paradigm proving able to create powerful capabilities for understanding not only text, but images, audio, and as is the case here, EM signals. This will both change the character of warfare as it makes it easier to build generic classifiers and generators for strategically relevant things, and it will likely also yield interesting and unforeseen scientific dividends a...

blogs.content:
Listen to this post:

 Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life.
 ―  Prince

 Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, 1993–2026

 Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted.

 In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA , convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT.

 ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain.

 Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation , notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle.

 Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing , and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit.

 That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation.

 Nvidia, Most Valuable Company in the World, 2024–2026

 Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA.

 LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter. The second is that Anthropic, which found funding from Amazon and Google, originally also-rans to the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, had to learn how to use Trainium chips from Amazon and TPUs from Google; this was difficult, but ultimately meant that the leading LLM did not have any Nvidia dependency at all (Anthropic runs on Nvidia chips, because they learned how to run on anything). The third is the most devastating: LLMs are so effective at writing software that any software-based moat will inevitably dry up.

 Nvidia’s second moat, its networking and systems approach, is more durable, although challenged by Google (and by extension, Anthropic) in particular. Nvidia’s systems approach is also the easy answer for enterprises and governments seeking to own their own hardware, and neoclouds seeking to build data centers that are independent of the hyperscalers. The latter market rents chips to both hyperscalers and frontier labs, as well as individual companies, but is challenged as obvious sources of power and political permission disappear. They also need money to afford Nvidia’s systems, which has increasingly come from Nvidia itself.

 Nvidia’s third moat is its mastery of the supply chain, and this is the moat that suddenly looks much more tenuous. Huang has bragged about the fact that he has never signed a contract with TSMC over their three decades of partnership; it’s a relationship built on a handshake and mutual trust with Huang specifically. This is, per the point above, a very Asian way of doing business, and Huang was the master of that. It’s questionable whether or not that trust and willingness to commit will persist when the handshake is no longer there.

 Nvidia’s most important moat, however, was the degree to which it was not a normal company. Huang organized Nvidia as an exoskeleton around one man: himself. There is very little management at Nvidia — Huang famously has 60 direct reports — for the same reason that there was no succession plan: Nvidia could move so quickly and so aggressively because the company still behaved as if it were a startup. Indeed, lots of established companies — including those still led by founders — claim to still be a startup, but only one, Nvidia, really was organized that way. That paid off with all of those successful bets; it also created an environment where there were no checks on Huang. And, now that he is gone, the exoskeleton is much more poised to collapse than you might expect.

 The AI Bubble, 2025–2027?

 The first part of the AI buildout was funded by free cash flow, particularly from the hyperscalers. Then, during the second half of last year, nearly everyone started turning to debt. Now — starting with Google this past summer — the primary funding mechanism is equity. In the long run, this should come full circle, and future build-outs will once again be funded by free cash flow, generated from the infrastructure that is being built now.

 The problem for Nvidia is that the companies most able to navigate this progression are the hyperscalers, which have the resources to challenge Nvidia’s hold on the chip market. To that end, Nvidia has been very eager to ensure that it is selling not only to the hyperscalers, but to other would-be competitors, like the neoclouds; there will likely, at some point, be serious questions raised about exactly how Nvidia went about allocating compute in pursuit of this goal.

 The neoclouds, however, are at a meaningful disadvantage when it comes to funding. First, their debt is significantly more expensive, given that their only business is renting GPUs (as opposed to, say, running the most valuable advertising businesses in the world, or the world’s largest e-commerce platform, or dominating enterprise software). Second, their equity is increasingly worthless, given the significant risks attached to that credit. If a neocloud can’t pay, it’s the equity holders that get wiped out first.

 This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business : Nvidia increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off.

 It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more supply to market.

 AI as Normal Technology and the U.S. Semiconductor Industry, 1947~2047

 Perhaps because he had been preaching the gospel of accelerated computing for so long, Huang was the leading figure pushing back against the doomer narrative surrounding AI. Yes, AI was a massive business opportunity, but it was still normal technology; the safety issues presented were engineering challenges to be solved. What required consideration was not just the next five years, but the next fifty. It’s a view that I am, in full disclosure, generally aligned with.

 Many others are not. On one hand there are the aforementioned doomers, certain that fast takeoff is imminent — or has already started — as AI increasingly builds better AI in a recursive loop. The end state is an AI that is massively more capable than humans, and uncontrollable by them; the only hope is to ensure that AI is aligned with humanity, by which adherents to this viewpoint mean aligned with them and their view of the world. This contingent is, broadly speaking, represented by Anthropic. And, in this view, actively working to enable and accelerate uncontrollable open weights models is a threat to humanity.

 On the other hand there are the China hawks, who view AI as a national security issue, and the key to U.S. military dominance in a world where China owns the means of production of most militarily relevant hardware. In this world giving China access to chips is effectively treason against the United States.

 For both of these groups, Huang was public enemy number one, because of his determinati...

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 9,924 new readers. The last time a board’s call sparked this kind of backlash? OpenAI’s firing of Sam Altman in 2023. Three years later, a swell of Nvidia employees and tech titans is hoping for a similar outcome for Jensen Huang.
 A petition demanding his return just topped 140K signatures in a matter of days, Elon Musk’s among them, and big investors want the door left open. Now, the Financial Times also says the man at the heart of it all has been privately mulling a comeback.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Musk, Nvidia staff rally to bring back Jensen Huang

 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 Turn a messy plan into a shared board

 Report: OpenAI folds robotics team into core research

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 JENSEN HUANG & NVIDIA
 🔄  Musk, Nvidia staff rally to bring back Jensen Huang
 Image source: X / petition website / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Elon Musk, Nvidia employees, and top investors are pushing Nvidia’s board to reconsider Jensen Huang’s exit, with an online petition to reinstate him passing 140K signatures days after the co-founder resigned amid multiple reported affairs.
 The details:
 The petition argues Huang was removed before any proof of spying surfaced or an outside probe even concluded, and calls for “due process, not mob justice.”

 Over 7,000 signers claim to be Nvidia staff, and in an earlier poll on anonymous app Blind, 88% of 232 Nvidia staffers said Huang should stay.

 Musk signed the petition, arguing Nvidia’s supply deals are exposed without Huang because “many… were a handshake with Jensen, not a contract.”

 The board has yet to respond publicly and is still picking a search firm, while reports say Huang has been “participating in the process” of picking his successor.

 A Financial Times report also revealed that Huang is privately weighing a return, with an ally building a “war room” of tech execs to help lobby for it.

 Why it matters: Nvidia is nothing without its people? The Jensen saga is entering its OpenAI-Altman moment, when staff and investor pressure got Sam his job back days after his ouster. Altman’s drama stayed mostly internal, while Jensen’s has spilled into geopolitics, Congress, and the FBI — but his backers are eyeing a similar resolution.

 TOGETHER WITH OPENART
 💬  Create ads in your AI assistant with OpenArt MCP

 The Rundown: OpenArt MCP brings OpenArt’s image and video ad tools into AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT. No prompt expertise needed: just describe what you want in simple language and share a product photo or link. Built-in skills ask for details, plan scripts and shots, and create a draft for you to review before a final version.
 With OpenArt MCP, you can:
 Turn a product photo or link into a product listing video or a TV-style commercial

 Turn one script into a creator ad, a polished presenter video, or a talking head

 Generate multiple ad variations at once with different hooks, headlines, or scenes

 Add OpenArt MCP .

 THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE
 💡  The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.
 Zach, Editor-in-Chief: As more of a creative type, I’ve never loved data analysis. Finding the right numbers used to take forever, and I wasn't even sure I was comparing the right things once I had them. Now I connect Claude to Beehiiv, our newsletter platform, and work through the numbers conversationally.
 Each week I have a scheduled task to run our stats report. Claude pulls open rates, clicks, reader ratings, comments, and more for all three of our newsletters, surfacing themes and notes across issues. I also built a filter to weed out bot clicks and fake poll votes, and I package it all into a page I present in our team meeting.
 The follow-up questions are where I really feel the value. With the data in front of me, I can keep poking at issues, ask for more, or troubleshoot on the fly in the same chat with the context already there.
 The connector has helped me dig into the data and run tests without my eyes glazing over, and made me more comfortable actually diving into an important area that I used to dread.
 Brooke, Community Engagement Lead: I run our support inbox solo, and the same questions kept coming up. I wanted my team to see what members were actually writing in about instead of it living in my head. I just finished building this with Claude connected to our Gmail support inbox, plus Slack and scheduled tasks.
 Every Thursday, Claude reads the week's support threads and filters out spam and noise. It groups the real member questions by theme, then by the team that can fix them. It drafts one short post per team covering the top thing members ran into and a suggested fix. I review, tweak, and send each post to that team's Slack channel before our Friday meeting.
 At the start of each month, Claude audits the full month of tickets: what drove volume, what changed from last month, and what's a product gap versus a one-off. It also checks my saved replies against what members actually asked. The goal is recurring tickets fixed at the source instead of answered over and over.

 AI TRAINING
 👨🏻‍🏫 Turn a messy plan into a shared board

 The Rundown: Claude Whiteboards turns a messy plan you talk through or paste into a board your team can edit. In this guide, you'll build one, check what Claude laid out, fix it, and share it with your team.
 Step-by-step:
 In Claude's sidebar, click Artifacts, then the Whiteboard tile under Make something new. A blank board opens

 Click Chat at the top of the board and talk your plan through with the microphone, or paste it in. Include owners and any dates you know

 Read Claude's reply and the board it builds. Claude fills gaps with its own guesses, so check every owner, date, and arrow against what you said

 Fix small things with the toolbar at the bottom. To rework one area, drag a box around it, click Chat in the toolbar, and describe the change

 Click Share, invite teammates by email, and choose Editor, Commenter, or Viewer. Invites start on Commenter

 Pro tip: Before you invite anyone, settle the dates Claude guessed with their owners. On our test board, two later tasks hung off one guessed date.
 Watch the full guide at The Rundown University →

 PRESENTED BY COLLIBRA
 👀  Your AI agents are working. Who’s watching?

 The Rundown: Agents now read, decide, and act across your tools, and the fleet grows whether you govern it or not. Drift, not hackers, is the usual failure. Collibra’s playbook shows how to scan every agent, set fleet-wide rules, and catch problems early.
 The playbook covers:
 How to build governance for autonomy to scale agents

 Where to start for your specific use case

 A 10-step plan and maturity self-assessment

 Get the playbook .

 OPENAI
 🤖  Report: OpenAI folds robotics team into core research
 Image source: Robocurve

 The Rundown: OpenAI moved its robotics team into its main research and product groups, according to Fortune, with the company saying GPT-6 Astra and other models can run robots without a separate brain — though staffers soon disputed the claim.
 The details:
 OpenAI says general models like GPT-6 Astra can be put to work on robots directly, instead of needing specialized or world models as previously thought.

 The company previously shuttered its robotics division in 2020 and rebooted it in 2024, with Sam Altman saying OpenAI is pursuing a humanoid of its own.

 Engineer David Schnurr called OpenAI robotics “alive and well” and pointed to 15 open roles, months after Sam Altman’s May hiring push for the team.

 Others also pushed back , with one staffer calling the report “completely wrong” and another saying OpenAI robotics still had the “same program, roadmap, goals.”

 Why it matters: This feels less like an “OpenAI isn’t prioritizing robotics” story and more like a “general models can do more than we anticipated” one. We’ve seen robotics breakthroughs across top labs. Now, with frontier models running things themselves, improving the robot’s brain may be a bigger research need than the hardware itself.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Nav built an AI tutoring tracker to see if lessons actually work
 Today's workflow comes from reader Nav :

“I'm a parent with two boys, one preparing for GCSEs and the other for the 11+ entrance exams, and they have several tutors covering Maths, English, Science and Music Theory. I wanted a better way to manage their education and to understand whether they were actually making progress. This is a parent-built system, not a commercial education product, and I developed it using AI tools without needing traditional software development skills.
 I record tutoring sessions and use Otter.ai to generate transcripts. I use ChatGPT to review the Otter transcripts, summarize each lesson, identify areas of weakness, extract homework, and recommend follow-up actions. It also compares feedback across sessions to see whether particular learning gaps are improving.
 On Fridays, I hold a progress checkpoint where ChatGPT helps review recent lessons, highlight learning gaps, identify overdue actions, and suggest what to prioritise with each tutor. The biggest benefit is that I'm no longer just paying for tutoring and hoping it's working.”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

blogs.content:
Read on tomtunguz.com →
 OpenAI & Anthropic each hold roughly 90% market share of an AI segment, but those segments are different : Anthropic holds dominant share at the premium end (94%), & OpenAI at the low end (81%). 1

 Across 10,000+ enterprises, that split raises a business question : is this a deliberate pricing strategy to capture different ends of the market, or a structural cost difference in how the two labs serve tokens?

 Anthropic sells a premium product & dominates the SOTA (state-of-the-art) tier. Anthropic’s share of SOTA token volume rose from 81% in July to 94% on November 2, propelled by the September 21 rollout of Claude Opus 5.5. 1 , 2 , 3

 The mid tier is where the two labs now collide directly. Across all Sonnet & Sol versions (Sonnet 5 & 5.5 vs GPT-6 Sol & 6.1 Sol), OpenAI climbed from 0% in July to 47% of mid-tier volume by November 2, & took 57% of the newest Sonnet 5.5 vs Sol 6/6.1 cohort within six weeks of launch. 1 , 4

 OpenAI pursued the opposite strategy, using aggressive price cuts on Luna to capture the high-volume floor. On July 30, OpenAI cut Luna pricing by 80% & then another 50% just a few months later, for a 90% total reduction. 5 , 6

 On September 22, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Luna at $0.10 per 1m tokens. 6 Its low-end share surged from 30% to 66% after the first cut, peaked at 84%, & finished at 81% on November 2. 1 , 7

 Open-weight token share climbed every week from 7% in July to 33% in September, then stalled at 31% in the same week GPT-6 Luna & Sol cut prices by 50%. 1 , 8

 That raises the strategic question in foundation models today : is Luna’s pricing a short-term market-share subsidy, or a structural cost advantage in OpenAI’s model architecture?

blogs.description: The demise of Jensen Huang was the end of a great many things, including Nvidia's long-term prospects, the AI bubble, and the exceptional way in which the U.S. viewed itself in the world.
blogs.content:
The demise of Jensen Huang was the end of a great many things, including Nvidia's long-term prospects, the AI bubble, and the exceptional way in which the U.S. viewed itself in the world.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life.
―  Prince

Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, 1993–2026

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted.

In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA , convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT.

ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain.

Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation , notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle.

Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing , and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit.

That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation.

Nvidia, Most Valuable Company in the World, 2024–2026

Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA.

LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter. The second is that Anthropic, which found funding from Amazon and Google, originally also-rans to the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, had to learn how to use Trainium chips from Amazon and TPUs from Google; this was difficult, but ultimately meant that the leading LLM did not have any Nvidia dependency at all (Anthropic runs on Nvidia chips, because they learned how to run on anything). The third is the most devastating: LLMs are so effective at writing software that any software-based moat will inevitably dry up.

Nvidia’s second moat, its networking and systems approach, is more durable, although challenged by Google (and by extension, Anthropic) in particular. Nvidia’s systems approach is also the easy answer for enterprises and governments seeking to own their own hardware, and neoclouds seeking to build data centers that are independent of the hyperscalers. The latter market rents chips to both hyperscalers and frontier labs, as well as individual companies, but is challenged as obvious sources of power and political permission disappear. They also need money to afford Nvidia’s systems, which has increasingly come from Nvidia itself.

Nvidia’s third moat is its mastery of the supply chain, and this is the moat that suddenly looks much more tenuous. Huang has bragged about the fact that he has never signed a contract with TSMC over their three decades of partnership; it’s a relationship built on a handshake and mutual trust with Huang specifically. This is, per the point above, a very Asian way of doing business, and Huang was the master of that. It’s questionable whether or not that trust and willingness to commit will persist when the handshake is no longer there.

Nvidia’s most important moat, however, was the degree to which it was not a normal company. Huang organized Nvidia as an exoskeleton around one man: himself. There is very little management at Nvidia — Huang famously has 60 direct reports — for the same reason that there was no succession plan: Nvidia could move so quickly and so aggressively because the company still behaved as if it were a startup. Indeed, lots of established companies — including those still led by founders — claim to still be a startup, but only one, Nvidia, really was organized that way. That paid off with all of those successful bets; it also created an environment where there were no checks on Huang. And, now that he is gone, the exoskeleton is much more poised to collapse than you might expect.

The AI Bubble, 2025–2027?

The first part of the AI buildout was funded by free cash flow, particularly from the hyperscalers. Then, during the second half of last year, nearly everyone started turning to debt. Now — starting with Google this past summer — the primary funding mechanism is equity. In the long run, this should come full circle, and future build-outs will once again be funded by free cash flow, generated from the infrastructure that is being built now.

The problem for Nvidia is that the companies most able to navigate this progression are the hyperscalers, which have the resources to challenge Nvidia’s hold on the chip market. To that end, Nvidia has been very eager to ensure that it is selling not only to the hyperscalers, but to other would-be competitors, like the neoclouds; there will likely, at some point, be serious questions raised about exactly how Nvidia went about allocating compute in pursuit of this goal.

The neoclouds, however, are at a meaningful disadvantage when it comes to funding. First, their debt is significantly more expensive, given that their only business is renting GPUs (as opposed to, say, running the most valuable advertising businesses in the world, or the world’s largest e-commerce platform, or dominating enterprise software). Second, their equity is increasingly worthless, given the significant risks attached to that credit. If a neocloud can’t pay, it’s the equity holders that get wiped out first.

This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business : Nvidia increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off.

It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more supply to market.

AI as Normal Technology and the U.S. Semiconductor Industry, 1947~2047

Perhaps because he had been preaching the gospel of accelerated computing for so long, Huang was the leading figure pushing back against the doomer narrative surrounding AI. Yes, AI was a massive business opportunity, but it was still normal technology; the safety issues presented were engineering challenges to be solved. What required consideration was not just the next five years, but the next fifty. It’s a view that I am, in full disclosure, generally aligned with.

Many others are not. On one hand there are the aforementioned doomers, certain that fast takeoff is imminent — or has already started — as AI increasingly builds better AI in a recursive loop. The end state is an AI that is massively more capable than humans, and uncontrollable by them; the only hope is to ensure that AI is aligned with humanity, by which adherents to this viewpoint mean aligned with them and their view of the world. This contingent is, broadly speaking, represented by Anthropic. And, in this view, actively working to enable and accelerate uncontrollable open weights models is a threat to humanity.

On the other hand there are the China hawks, who view AI as a national security issue, and the key to U.S. military dominance in a world where China owns the means of production of most militarily rel...
